77-019.r: Bokaro Thermal Power Station → Bokaro district, Jharkhand.

77-020.r: Integrated steel plant at Kalinganagar, Jajpur (Odisha) → run by Tata Steel, not Steel Authority of India (per the book's explanation).
77-020.c: The book prints (a) as correctly matched, but its own explanation says the Jajpur plant is Tata Steel's, not SAIL's; Kayamkulam is an NTPC plant, which fits (d).

77-021.r: Barh Super Thermal Power Station → Patna district, Bihar; approved capacity 3300 MW, installed 1320 MW; Unit 4 in 2014, Unit 5 in 2016.

77-022.r: Wrong pair: Korba–Wind; Korba is a thermal power station. Correct: Patratu–thermal, Jhakri–hydroelectric, Kalpakkam–nuclear.

78-001.r: India's first nuclear power station → Tarapur (near Boisar, Thane district, Maharashtra); commercial operation from 1969.

78-002.r: Nuclear share of power in 2006-2007 →between 3 and 4% (about 3%). Now (31 December 2025): 8780 MW, only 1.71% of installed capacity (513729.69 MW).

78-004.r: India is self-sufficient in thorium, extracted mostly from monazite; uranium is the main nuclear fuel.

78-005.r: Nuclear stations: Kota (Rawatbhata) → Rajasthan; Tarapur → Maharashtra; Kakrapara → Gujarat; Narora → Uttar Pradesh.

78-007.r: Commissioning years: Kota 1973, Kalpakkam 1984, Kakrapara 1993, Kaiga 2000 → every printed pair is wrong; the book gives no single answer (*).

78-008.r: Nuclear energy → promising for future demand (A true). But nuclear minerals aren't everywhere: uranium is scarce and imported; thorium is abundant but localised (R false).

78-009.r: Thal → Maharashtra; Manuguru → Andhra Pradesh (now Telangana); Kakrapara → Gujarat; Kaiga → Karnataka.

78-010.r: Wrong pair: Ennore–Meghalaya; Ennore is in Tamil Nadu. Correct: Kaiga–Karnataka, Rawatbhata–Rajasthan, Muppandal–Tamil Nadu.

78-011.r: Kudankulam (Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu) → site for two 1000 MW nuclear plants; marked B on the map.

78-013.r: Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu) → Russia agreed to six reactor units (answer); the first Inter-Government Agreement (1988, Gorbachev) was for two reactors.

78-014.r: India's 25th nuclear plant → Rawatbhata, Rajasthan (construction began July 2011).

78-015.r: India's twentieth nuclear power station → Kaiga, Karnataka.

78-016.r: Kalpakkam has no heavy water plant. Heavy water plants: Hazira, Vadodara (Gujarat), Kota (Rajasthan), Manuguru (Telangana), Talcher (Odisha), Thal (Maharashtra), Tuticorin (Tamil Nadu).

78-017.r: Mithivirdi nuclear plant (Talaja, Bhavnagar, Gujarat) → with the USA, under the Indo-US nuclear deal of 2008.

78-018.r: Anushakti Vidyut Nigam Ltd → joint venture of NPCIL (51%) and NTPC (49%); incorporated 27 January 2011.

78-019.r: Wrong pair: Haripur–Haryana; Haripur is in West Bengal. Correct: Jaitapur–Maharashtra, Mithi Virdi–Gujarat, Kovvada–Andhra Pradesh.

78-020.r: Two wrong pairs, so the book gives (a) and (b): Kaiga is in Karnataka, Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu. Correct: Kakrapar–Gujarat, Kudankulam–Tamil Nadu.

78-021.r: Installed nuclear capacity (book): Kakrapar 1840 MW, Tarapur 1400, Kaiga 880, Narora 440; the book's answer is Tarapur.
78-021.c: Tarapur (1400 MW) was right when asked in 2021; with its two new large units now running, Kakrapar (1840 MW) has the bigger installed capacity today.

79-001.r: Koyna (Maharashtra) → hydroelectric project on the Koyna river, run by the Maharashtra State Electricity Board.

79-002.r: Rana Pratap Sagar hydel power station → Rawatbhata, beside the Rana Pratap Sagar Dam; built with Canada's help.

79-003.r: Jawahar Sagar hydroelectric project → Chambal river, Rajasthan; part of the Chambal Valley development plan.

79-004.r: Rana Pratap Sagar Dam → gravity masonry dam on the Chambal at Rawatbhata, Rajasthan.

79-005.r: Hydro share of electricity → about 10% (10.6% in 2016-17). Installed capacity, 31 December 2025: hydro 50914.66 MW of 513729.69 MW.

80-001.r: Pavagada (Karnataka) → solar; Tattapani (Chhattisgarh) → geothermal; Muppandal (Tamil Nadu) → wind; Kakrapar (Gujarat) → atomic.

80-002.r: Highest solar energy potential → Rajasthan (MNRE, as of 31 December 2025).

80-003.r: Chamera (Ravi river, Chamba, HP) → hydro; Gwal Pahari (Gurugram, Haryana) → solar; Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu) → atomic; Patratu (Ramgarh, Jharkhand) → thermal.

80-004.r: Satara (Maharashtra) → known for the Chalkewadi wind energy project.

80-005.r: Wind potential (GW, 120 m / 150 m): Gujarat 142.56 / 180.8, Rajasthan 127.75 / 284.2, Tamil Nadu 68.75 / 95.1; India 695.50 / 1163.9 → Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.

80-006.r: Wind power capacity (31 December 2025): Gujarat 1st, Tamil Nadu 2nd.

80-007.r: Wrong statement: non-conventional sources give less than 1% of commercial energy; they actually give more than 1%.

80-008.r: Asia's biggest wind project when asked → Muppandal, Tamil Nadu (150 MW).

80-009.r: Largest tidal energy area in India → Khambhat (Cambay) coast.

80-010.r: Main tidal energy area → Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay); India's gulfs and estuaries have tides strong enough to turn turbines.

80-011.r: Most tidal potential → Bhavnagar (answer). Best sites: Gulf of Cambay and Gulf of Kutch (west coast), Ganges delta–Sundarbans (east); Cambay and Kutch most attractive.

80-012.r: NHPC (National Hydroelectric Power Corporation, set up 1975) → electricity generation: hydropower, later geothermal, tidal, wind.

80-013.r: Gujarat → first in installed capacity and generation of electricity (when asked); still 1st in gross installed capacity (31 December 2025).

80-014.r: India's per capita energy use, 1994 → about 243 kg oil equivalent (book: 244 kg), far below the world's 1471 kg.

80-015.r: Rampura → first Indian village with its own solar power plant, in Uttar Pradesh.
